 GTA and the psychology of breaking rules: Why people who follow rules in real life enjoy virtual freedom, rebellion and the thrill of doing things they would never attempt outside a video game

 Print The wait for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) is finally over. Released on November 19, 2026, the latest instalment in Rockstar Games' hugely popular franchise brings players back to the fictional world of Vice City, with a new storyline centred on Jason Duval and Lucia. For millions of fans, the excitement is about exploring a new map, discovering hidden details and getting behind the wheel after a very long time, which is infact several decades. But there is another reason the GTA franchise has held people's attention for so long: the freedom to break rules without having to deal with real-world consequences. There is a curious contradiction about playing Grand Theft Auto (GTA). Someone who patiently waits for a green traffic signal, follows workplace rules and avoids getting into trouble in everyday life might happily spend an evening speeding through virtual streets, stealing cars, escaping police chases and creating complete chaos in a video game. And they might enjoy every minute of it. Why does breaking rules feel so entertaining when most people spend their real lives trying to avoid trouble? The answer has less to do with wanting to become a criminal and more to do with how people experience freedom, curiosity, control and consequences. GTA offers something that everyday life rarely does, which is an environment where players can experiment with behaviour without facing the real-world consequences of their actions. It allows them to step into a world where the usual boundaries do not always apply. Why GTA makes rule-breaking so entertaining
 Unlike games that push players through a fixed sequence of missions, GTA gives them a large virtual world to explore. Players can follow the storyline, drive around the city, discover hidden locations or simply ignore the main mission and see what happens when they cause trouble. That freedom matters psychologically. A 2006 study published in Motivation and Emotion, titled The Motivational Pull of Video Games: A Self-Determination Theory Approach, examined why people enjoy playing video games. Researchers Richard Ryan, C. Scott Rigby and Andrew Przybylski found that the enjoyment of the players was associated with three psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. GTA taps particularly well into that first need. Players are not constantly told what to do. They can decide how to spend their time, which routes to take and how much trouble they want to get into. Even when the game has missions and objectives, the open-world environment leaves room for experimentation. And sometimes, doing absolutely nothing related to the main storyline is the most entertaining part. The thrill of doing something you normally wouldn't
 Think about the ordinary restrictions of daily life. There are traffic rules, workplace expectations, social boundaries and consequences attached to almost every decision. Most people learn to regulate their behaviour because they understand that their actions affect others. A video game creates a different setting. A player can drive recklessly through a virtual city, provoke a police chase or attempt something completely absurd without putting an actual person or vehicle in danger. The distinction between virtual actions and real-world behaviour is important here. Enjoying a fictional act does not automatically mean someone wants to repeat it outside the game. In fact, part of the attraction may be the knowledge that it is pretend. Players can explore an exaggerated version of rebellion while remaining aware that they are interacting with a fictional environment. A 2010 study published in the Journal of Communication, titled It's Okay to Shoot a Character: Moral Disengagement in Violent Video Games, examined and studied why players and participants enjoy virtual violence. Researchers Tilo Hartmann and Peter Vorderer found that familiarity with violent games and the perception that the activity was simply a game could reduce feelings of guilt and negative emotions during play. That helps explain why someone can enjoy a chaotic GTA session without necessarily carrying those attitudes into everyday life. Join conversation

 Why breaking the game's rules becomes another game
 There is another interesting part of GTA: the game actually gives players rules to break. For instance, a police chase introduces a new challenge. The player must escape, avoid being caught and find ways to survive. This is where the feeling of competence comes in. Players are not just doing something forbidden; they are testing their ability to handle the consequences within the game. Research published in Computers in Human Behavior has also explored how game feedback, rules and social interaction influence enjoyment of the players and make them feel more capable and invested in the experience. In GTA, escaping a police chase or completing a difficult mission can provide a sense of achievement. The challenge is part of the fun.
